title: Variables and Data Types
text:
Variables — What Are They?

This slide is the conceptual foundation — no syntax, no types, no code yet. The only goal is to give students an intuitive mental model before anything else. Programs need to remember things: a score, a name, a temperature. A variable is just a named place to hold one piece of information. The scoreboard and sticky-note examples are deliberately mundane — the point is that this idea already exists in everyday life. Students already understand “Score: 47” as a label paired with a value. That’s all a variable is.

Before a program can do anything useful, it needs to remember things.
Think about situations where you already use named values without thinking about it:

A scoreboard: Score: 47 — the word “Score” is the label; 47 is what’s stored there right now
A thermostat: Temperature: 68°F — same idea
A name badge: Name: Alice — a label that identifies what the value means

A variable is the same thing inside a program:

A variable is a named container that holds one piece of information.

Your program can:

Store a value in it
Look at what’s currently inside
Change it whenever needed

That’s it. Everything else — types, syntax, declarations — is just the details of how Java makes you write this down.

title: Variables and Data Types
text:
Why Do Programs Need Variables?

The recipe analogy works well here — and keep it as plain text, no code. A recipe hardcoded for 2 people has to be rewritten by hand every time you want to change the serving size. With a variable, you change one number and every quantity updates. The point is conceptual: variables let one set of instructions work for many different inputs. The code version of this will make sense once students have seen declarations, printing, and arithmetic.

Imagine a recipe written for exactly 2 people:
- 2 cups of flour
- 1 cup of sugar
- 3 eggs
Want to make it for 4? You cross everything out and rewrite it.
Now imagine a version with a note at the top:
Servings: 2

- [servings] cups of flour
- [servings / 2] cups of sugar
- [servings * 2 - 1] eggs
Change the one number at the top → every quantity updates automatically.
That note at the top is a variable. One change, everywhere.

title: Variables and Data Types
text:
Variables in Algebra vs. Programming

Students have seen variables in algebra — start there. The similarities are real and worth naming: a variable is a named placeholder for a value. Then get into the differences. In algebra, the variable is unknown and you solve for it. In programming, you are the one who sets the value — the computer doesn’t “solve” for anything. Also: algebra variables are almost always single letters; programming variables have full descriptive names. And the biggest one: in programming, a variable’s value can change.

You have seen variables before — in algebra.

The core idea is the same. The rules are different.

title: Variables and Data Types
section: Think of Variables as Labeled Cups
text:
Think of Variables as Labeled Cups

The Starbucks analogy is intuitive and memorable. At a Starbucks counter, your cup has your name written on it (so the barista knows whose order it is), a size (tall, grande, venti — that’s the type), and whatever drink is actually inside (the value). A variable works exactly the same way. The name identifies it. The type says what kind of thing it can hold. The value is what’s actually in there right now. And just like a cup can be emptied and refilled, a variable’s value can change.

When you order at Starbucks, your cup has three things:

Your name written on it — so the barista knows whose it is
A size — tall, grande, venti — that determines what it can hold
The actual drink inside

A variable works the same way:

And just like a cup can be emptied and refilled — a variable’s value can change.

title: Variables and Data Types
text:
Why Do Variables Have Types?

The food container analogy gets at the intuition. Different foods need different containers — you wouldn’t put soup in a paper bag. The container type isn’t arbitrary: it’s determined by what you’re storing. Same with data. Types tell the computer what kind of data the variable holds, which determines what operations make sense on it.

Different foods need different containers:



Coffee → cup
Burger → box or wrapper
Fries → paper bag
Ice cream → cone or cup


You wouldn’t put soup in a paper bag. The container depends on what you’re storing.

Data is the same way:

title: Variables and Data Types
section: The Assignment Operator — Not What You Think
text:
The Assignment Operator — Not What You Think

This is a genuine conceptual stumbling block. In mathematics, = means “these two things are equal.” In Java, = means “take the value on the right and store it in the variable on the left.” They look the same but behave completely differently. The clearest demonstration is a = a + 1: mathematically nonsense (subtract a from both sides: 0 = 1), but in programming it’s completely normal and means “add 1 to whatever is currently in a”. Do this on the board slowly: if a was 5, evaluate the right side (5+1=6), then store 6 into a. Now a is 6.

In algebra, = means “these are equal” — a statement of fact.
In Java, = means “store this value” — a command.
These are completely different things.


Algebra:
a = a + 1
Subtract a from both sides:
0 = 1   ← impossible

Java:
a = a + 1;
“Take the current value of a, add 1 to it, store the result back in a.”


int a = 5;
a = a + 1;           // a is now 6
a = a + 1;           // a is now 7
IO.println(a);       // prints 7

text:
Reassigning Variables

Show that a variable holds the MOST RECENT value assigned to it. Trace through the program step by step — this is a good opportunity to introduce the idea of tracing, which will be a recurring skill throughout the course. Emphasize: println shows what’s in the variable at that moment in time, not some average or history.

Once declared, a variable’s value can be changed:
int score = 0;
IO.println(score);       // prints 0

score = 10;
IO.println(score);       // prints 10

score = score + 5;
IO.println(score);       // prints 15
The variable always holds the most recently assigned value.
Let’s trace it step by step:

title: Variables and Data Types
text:
What Is Input?

Pure concept — no code yet. Students already know about output (IO.println sends information from the program to the screen). Input is the other direction: information flows from the user to the program. The two-arrow figure makes this concrete. Spend time here — the mental model of “two directions of information flow” is foundational for everything interactive they will ever write.

So far, information has only flowed one direction:

Program → Screen — using IO.println

Input is the other direction:

User → Program — the user types something; the program receives it



Output (IO.println)
The program sends information out. The screen shows it.

Input (IO.readln)
The user types information in. The program receives it.

Together, these two directions let you write programs that have a conversation with the user.

title: Variables and Data Types
text:
IO.readln — The Simplest Form

Introduce the mechanics first, without a prompt string — so students can focus entirely on what readln DOES. When Java hits IO.readln(), execution stops. A cursor blinks. The program waits. The user types something and presses Enter. Whatever they typed is produced as a String. That’s it. Walk through the sample run line by line. Emphasize: the program is paused — it is not broken, it is not slow, it is waiting for the user.

IO.readln() pauses the program and waits for the user to type a line of text.
void main() {
    String name = IO.readln();
    IO.println(name);
}
When Java reaches IO.readln():

The program stops
A cursor appears — the program is waiting
The user types something and presses Enter
IO.readln produces the typed text as a String
That String is stored in name
The program continues

Sample run:
Alice
Alice






Warning


If you do not store the result in a variable, it is gone the instant the line finishes — the program read the input and immediately forgot it.

title: Variables and Data Types
Variables and Data Types
text:
Adding a Prompt

The no-prompt form works but is confusing in practice — users see a blank screen and have no idea what to type. The prompt string solves this. It is printed before the program pauses, giving the user a cue. Key point: the prompt does not change what gets produced — it is purely for the human’s benefit. Show a side-by-side comparison of sample runs so the difference is vivid. This is the form students will use in all their programs.

Without a prompt, the user just sees a blinking cursor — and has no idea what to type.
IO.readln accepts an optional prompt: a message to display before waiting.
void main() {
    String name = IO.readln("What is your name? ");
    IO.println(name);
}
Sample run:
What is your name? Alice
Alice
The prompt is printed first — then the program pauses for input.


Without prompt:
▌
(User sees a blank cursor — confused)

With prompt:
What is your name? ▌
(User knows exactly what to type)







Note


The prompt does not affect what the program receives. It is a message for the user, not part of the input.









Note


IO.readln always produces a String — even if the user types 42, the program receives the text "42", not the number. Converting it to a number is coming in the next lecture.

Variables and Data Types
text:
Why Does the Type Matter?

Now that students have written declarations and feel some comfort with the syntax, this slide gives the intuition for why types exist — without any technical jargon. The key point: the type changes what operations make sense. You can add two ints. You can’t add two names. The computer uses the type to figure out what “+” even means.

2 + 3 and 2.0 + 3.0 look the same to us. The computer handles them differently.

2 + 3 — whole-number addition. The result is always exact.
2.0 + 3.0 — decimal addition. Works differently, and can occasionally produce small surprises.

IO.println(0.1 + 0.2);   // you might expect 0.3 ...
                          // the computer prints 0.30000000000000004
This is not a bug — it’s just how decimal math works on a computer.
The type also tells the computer which operations make sense:

You can multiply two int values.
You cannot multiply two String values — what would "Alice" * "Bob" even mean?


The type is not just a label for you. It tells the computer what kind of thing the variable holds.

title: Variables and Data Types
section: Should You Always Use double for Numbers?
text:
Should You Always Use double for Numbers?

Students sometimes wonder: if double can hold whole numbers too (5.0 is a valid double), why ever use int? The key reasons are semantic clarity and the decimal surprise shown above. Don’t mention memory or performance — that’s too deep for this stage. Focus on meaning: an int says “this is always a whole number.” That’s both clearer and safer.

double can store whole numbers too — 5.0 is perfectly valid.
So why use int at all?
Whole numbers stay exact. Decimal math can have small surprises (see previous slide). If a value is always a whole number, int guarantees it stays clean.
The type says what you mean.
double numberOfStudents = 2.7;  // What does this even mean?
int numberOfStudents = 27;      // Clear and correct
You cannot have 2.7 students. Using int communicates that — and if you accidentally compute a decimal result, Java will warn you.






Tip


Rule of thumb: Use int for things you count. Use double for things you measure.

Count: students, quiz scores, laps → int
Measure: temperature, GPA, price → double

title: Variables and Data Types
text:
Common Mistakes

These are the mistakes you will see most frequently in the first few weeks. Go through each one briefly and show what error it produces or what wrong output it causes. The goal is to make students recognize these errors when they see them, not to memorize a list.

1. Using a variable before giving it a value
int score;
IO.println(score);   // ERROR — score has no value yet
2. Wrong type for the value
int name = "Alice";   // ERROR — can't store text in an int
3. Forgetting to store IO.readln’s result
IO.readln("Enter your name: ");   // the returned value is lost
IO.println(name);                 // ERROR — name was never declared
4. Confusing = (assignment) with equality
score = 10;    // stores 10 in score ✓
score == 10;   // checks if score equals 10 — but does nothing here (coming later)
5. Case errors
int playerScore = 0;
IO.println(PlayerScore);   // ERROR — Java is case-sensitive

title: Introduction
text:
Your First Week at StreamBase



Imagine you just started a data engineering internship at StreamBase, a fast-growing streaming startup.




Your manager pulls you aside Monday morning:



“StreamBase has 200 million subscribers. Every stream, pause, skip, and rating gets logged — we’re sitting on 80 billion events in our data lake. The content licensing team meets in December and they need to know: which genres and films should we prioritize next quarter? That question requires distributed processing — one machine can’t touch 80 billion rows. We use HDFS and Spark for exactly this. Your job: build and validate the pipeline on a 100K-row sample first. If the aggregations are right and the dashboard answers the question, we scale it up. The code doesn’t change. Only the data does. Demo is December 11.”



You’d probably say: “Sure — what’s HDFS? What’s Spark?”

Timing: 4 min. Pause after the quote. Let it land. Ask: “How many of you know what HDFS is? Spark? MongoDB? A REST API?” Nobody should raise their hand.

title: Introduction
section: Why This Should Sound Like Gibberish
text:
Why This Should Sound Like Gibberish
That’s the correct reaction — and the whole point of this course.

HDFS, Spark, and MongoDB are all tools for working with data that doesn’t fit on one machine. You’ll meet each one by name later this semester: HDFS in Module 3, Spark in Module 4, MongoDB in Module 5.
The manager’s ask sounds intimidating because of the number — 80 billion events. But notice the actual instruction: build and validate on a 100K-row sample first.
The key idea for the entire course: the code you write for 100,000 rows is the same code that runs on 80 billion rows. Distributed tools are built so the program doesn’t change size with the data — only the number of machines running it does.
You are not learning toy versions of these tools. You are learning the real tools, on data small enough to fit in your head.


Timing: 4 min. This slide used to live only in speaker notes — it’s promoted to a real slide because “the code doesn’t change, only the scale does” is the single idea that makes the rest of the semester make sense, and students need it to study from, not just hear once.

title: Introduction
section: Why Can’t We Just Use Excel?
text:
Why Can’t We Just Use Excel?
80 billion rows. One machine. One core. Let’s do the arithmetic.


A laptop with 16 GB of RAM can hold roughly 200 million integers in memory at once.
80 billion rows is 400× that — you would need on the order of 400 machines just to store the data, before any processing starts.
Even if it fit, processing 80 billion rows sequentially at a generous 1 million rows/second would take over 22 hours — for one pass over the data, one time.



Distributed computing is the answer: split the data across many machines, process each machine’s chunk in parallel, then combine the results. That’s literally what HDFS (storage) and Spark (processing) exist to do — and it’s why this course spends three modules on them.

Timing: 4 min. Keep this to the arithmetic — it’s meant to be a quick, visceral “oh, that’s why” moment. The deeper “why parallel hardware exists at all” question is the next slide.

title: Introduction
section: Why Now? Clock Speeds & the Multicore Turn
text:
Why Now? Clock Speeds & the Multicore Turn
This isn’t a new problem tools just recently got good at solving — it’s a hardware story you can trace from what you already know.

From the 1970s to roughly 2005, CPUs got faster mainly by raising clock speed — more cycles per second, every year, like clockwork (literally).
Around 2005 that stopped. Faster clock speeds mean more heat, and chips had hit a thermal wall: you cannot dissipate the heat a much-faster single core would generate at a size that fits in a laptop.
The industry’s answer wasn’t “wait for a breakthrough” — it was stop making one core faster, and put more cores on the chip instead. Your laptop’s 8 or 16 cores are a direct consequence of that 2005 pivot.
Consequence for you as a programmer: the hardware is already parallel. A program that only ever uses one core is leaving most of the machine idle. Learning to write code that uses multiple cores isn’t optional specialization anymore — it’s how you use the hardware you already own.


Timing: 5 min. Ask first, before giving the answer: “Does anyone know why your laptop has multiple cores instead of one really fast core?” Let a guess or two land, then confirm with the thermal-wall explanation. This is the one moment all semester that connects directly to computer organization — transistors, clock cycles, heat — spend the full 5 minutes, don’t compress it.

title: Introduction
text:
Netflix: One Answer, 200 Million Times

Every subscriber’s homepage is personalized — Netflix computes a different ranked list of titles for each of its 200 million subscribers, and recomputes it continuously as viewing behavior changes.
Those rankings are trained on billions of individual signals: ratings, watches, pauses, skips, even how long you hovered over a title before clicking.
Put those together: 200 million personalized answers, each depending on a model trained on billions of events, updated continuously. No single machine reads billions of events and produces 200 million distinct outputs fast enough to matter — this is an aggregation-and-machine-learning problem that requires many machines working at once.


Timing: 4 min. The number that matters is 200 million distinct answers, not one shared answer computed once. Don’t get pulled into explaining how recommendation algorithms work — the point is scale, not ML technique.

title: Introduction
section: Google: The Problem That Started It All
text:
Google: The Problem That Started It All

In 2004, Google faced a concrete problem: index and rank the entire web — billions of pages, far more text than any one machine could even read through, let alone process into a searchable index.
Their solution was to split the job across thousands of ordinary machines, each handling a slice of the web, with a common pattern for combining partial results into one answer. They published this pattern as a paper: “MapReduce: Simplified Data Processing on Large Clusters.”
That single paper is the reason Module 3 of this course exists. In a few weeks you will write a MapReduce job yourself, using the exact pattern Google described in 2004 — it’s not a historical curiosity, it’s the design underneath Hadoop and, indirectly, Spark.


Timing: 4 min. Say “Module 3” out loud — a direct forward-reference, not a vague “later in the course.” Worth noting explicitly that this is 20-year-old, still-load-bearing computer science, not a dated example.

title: Introduction
text:
Amazon: Black Friday

On Black Friday, Amazon processes thousands of orders per second — and many of those orders are competing to read and write the same piece of data: how many units of a given item are left in stock.
A single database server handling that load has two bad options: fall behind and get too slow to be usable, or let two operations touch the same data at once and corrupt it — for example, two customers both “successfully” buying the last unit of an item that only had one left.
The fix is to spread both the data and the load across many machines — techniques called replication and sharding, which you’ll see in detail in Module 5. For now, just notice the shape of the problem: multiple things touching the same data at the same instant, with no one in charge of ordering them. Hold onto that shape — it is exactly the problem this entire module is about, just at the scale of two threads instead of two machines.


Timing: 5 min, the longest of the three vignettes. The last sentence is a deliberate, explicit plant for Session 3’s race conditions — say it clearly rather than leaving it implicit, since this slide is what students will re-read when race conditions are introduced and should recognize the connection themselves.

title: Introduction
text:
Parallel vs. Distributed: Two Kitchens
You’ll hear both words all semester. They are not the same thing, and the difference sets the shape of this whole course.

Parallel = one kitchen, many cooks. Everyone shares the same counters, the same stove, the same ingredients — reaching into the same space at the same time. This is Module 1: multiple threads inside a single running program, sharing the same memory.
Distributed = many separate kitchens, coordinating over the phone. Each kitchen has its own space and equipment; nothing is shared directly, everything that crosses between them is sent as an explicit message. This is Modules 2 through 6: separate machines, each with their own memory, coordinating over a network.


Timing: 4 min. State both definitions plainly and let them sit — the payoff slide is next.

title: Introduction
text:
Keep This Picture in Mind


For the next three weeks, every time this deck says “thread,” picture a cook in a shared kitchen — reaching for the same counter, the same stove, sometimes at the exact same moment as another cook. That collision is where every bug in this module comes from.

Timing: 3 min, closing the session. This is the standing analogy for the whole module — end class on this line so it’s the thing students carry into Session 2, where “process = kitchen, thread = cook” becomes the literal framing of the next lecture.

Course Description
Official catalog description:

This course will study the tools, techniques and architectures to provide hardware acceleration of software. Topics include: high-level synthesis, register transfer level descriptions and synthesis, gate and transistor level descriptions, finite state machines, systolic arrays and pipeline architectures. Both Field Programmable Gate Array (FPGA) and custom integrated circuit approaches will be covered. In addition to the application of Electronic Design Automation (EDA) tools, the algorithms they use will be described.

Course focus, Fall 2026:
This course introduces the architectures and programming models behind modern General-Purpose Graphics Processing Unit (GPGPU) computing. As the demand for computational throughput has outpaced what traditional single-core processors can deliver, GPUs have become the engine behind machine learning, scientific simulation, and real-time graphics. Acceleration teaches you to think and program in parallel - shifting from the “one instruction at a time” model of introductory programming to orchestrating thousands of threads working simultaneously on the same problem. The course uses Python and industry-relevant GPU frameworks (Numba CUDA, CuPy, PyTorch) throughout, delivered via Google Colab, so no prior experience with systems languages is required.

title: Python for Java Developers
text:
Same Logic, Different Grammar

You already know how to program: variables, loops, conditionals, functions — that thinking transfers completely
What’s different is syntax — the words and punctuation Python expects instead of Java’s
Today is a translation exercise, not a “learn programming from scratch” lecture
Goal by the end of class: read any short Python snippet and know what it does, even before you’ve memorized every keyword


~2 min. Reassure the room explicitly — many students hearing “new language” panic unnecessarily. Frame this as vocabulary, not new concepts.

title: Python for Java Developers
text:
No More Type Declarations


Java
int count = 5;
double price = 9.99;
String name = "Ada";
boolean done = false;

Python
count = 5
price = 9.99
name = "Ada"
done = False


Python infers the type from the value — you never write int, double, or String before a variable
The variable can even change type later (usually a bad idea, but Python allows it — Java does not)
Capitalization matters: Python’s True/False/None, not Java’s true/false/null


~3 min. Live-type this in a Colab cell rather than just showing it — run type(count), then reassign count = "five" and run type(count) again to make the “types are not fixed” point concrete.

title: Python for Java Developers
text:
Dynamic Typing: The Grammar-Teacher Analogy

Java is a strict grammar teacher: before you say a sentence, you must announce what part of speech every word is going to be — noun, verb, adjective — and the teacher checks you announced correctly before you’re allowed to speak
Python assumes you know what you mean, and figures out the parts of speech from context as you go
Trade-off: Java catches certain mistakes before the program ever runs (compile-time). Python only discovers a mismatch when that line actually executes (run-time) — so Python programs can fail later and more unexpectedly than Java ones
This is why Python code tends to look shorter — but it also means you need to test what you write more carefully


~3 min. This analogy is worth landing well — it explains why Python looks so sparse compared to Java without requiring any compiler-theory vocabulary the students don’t have.

text:
Lists: Java’s ArrayList, Python’s list


Java
ArrayList<Integer> nums =
    new ArrayList<>();
nums.add(10);
nums.add(20);
nums.get(0);
nums.size();

Python
nums = [10, 20]
nums.append(30)
nums[0]
len(nums)


Python’s list is built into the language — no import, no <Integer> type parameter
A single Python list can hold mixed types ([1, "two", 3.0]) — Java’s ArrayList<Integer> cannot
len(nums) is a function call, not a method — this is a common early typo (nums.len() does not exist)


~3 min. The “mixed types allowed” point is worth a live demo — it looks alarming to a Java developer at first. Note explicitly that NumPy arrays (Session 3) are not like this — they go back to Java’s “one type only” discipline, for reasons we’ll cover then.

title: Python for Java Developers
text:
List Slicing
nums = [10, 20, 30, 40, 50]

nums[1:3]     # [20, 30]   — index 1 up to (not including) index 3
nums[:2]      # [10, 20]   — from the start up to index 2
nums[3:]      # [40, 50]   — from index 3 to the end
nums[-1]      # 50         — negative index counts from the end
nums[::2]     # [10, 30, 50] — every 2nd element

Slicing has no Java equivalent — closest is manually looping and copying into a new array
The pattern [start:stop:step] — memorize this now, because NumPy array slicing (Session 3) uses exactly the same syntax


~3 min. Emphasize the last bullet strongly — this slide is deliberately positioned as direct setup for Session 3. Have students predict nums[1:-1] before revealing the answer.

title: Python for Java Developers
text:
None vs. null, and Truthiness
result = None          # Python's "no value" — like Java's null

if result:              # careful: 0, "", [], and None are all "falsy"
    print("has a value")
else:
    print("nothing here")

None is Python’s null — same idea, different capitalization and spelling
Java only treats null itself as special in an if. Python additionally treats 0, 0.0, "" (empty string), and [] (empty list) as “falsy” in an if — this has no Java parallel and causes real bugs
Rule of thumb: if you mean “is this specifically None,” write if result is None:, not just if result:


~2 min. This is a genuine gotcha, not a style note — an empty list silently behaving like “false” surprises every Java developer at least once. Worth a quick live example: if []:  print("shown"); else: print("not shown").

title: Python for Java Developers
text:
List Comprehensions: Thinking in Expressions


The loop way
squares = []
for x in range(10):
    squares.append(x ** 2)

The Pythonic way
squares = [x ** 2 for x in range(10)]


Both produce the exact same list — the second is Python’s idiomatic shorthand for “build a new list from a rule”
Read it right-to-left: “for x in range(10),” “compute x squared,” “collect into a list”
You’ll see this pattern constantly in other people’s Python code this semester — recognize it even if you don’t write it yet


~3 min. Don’t require fluency writing these yet — just reading comprehension. This slide is also a deliberate bridge: next session, NumPy will replace both versions above with x ** 2 on a whole array, no loop or comprehension at all.

text:
Why This Matters for GPU Programming

Python’s flexibility (no type declarations, quick to write) is exactly why we prototype in it
But that same flexibility has a cost: a Python for loop is checking and re-checking types on every single iteration — work a compiled Java loop never has to do
Next session, we’ll measure that cost, and meet the tool (NumPy) that removes it — which is also the first step toward the GPU way of thinking


~2 min. This is the bridge slide into Session 3 — plant “loops are secretly expensive” as a question, don’t answer it yet. Session 3 answers it with a real analogy and (in Lab 2/CK-2) real numbers.

Putting It All Together — A Rudimentary Database
Here’s what we just built:
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐

text:
Beyond the ArrayList
You already know ArrayList — a list that stores items in order, allows duplicates, and lets you access by index.
But sometimes you need something different:


“Does my list contain this username already?”


“What is the phone number for ‘Alice’?”


“Make sure no value appears twice.”



For these questions, ArrayList works — but there are better tools for the job: Sets and Maps.

title: Maps and Sets in Java

What is a Set?
A Set is a collection that:

Stores no duplicates — adding something that’s already there does nothing
Has no guaranteed order (unlike a list)
Lets you quickly ask: “Is this value in the set?”


Think of a set of student IDs — each ID either is in the set or it isn’t. You never want the same ID twice.

title: A* Search
text:
Where We’ve Been
You already know:

Backtracking — explore, undo, try another way
Pruning — skip branches that can’t possibly work


Question: In backtracking, when you have multiple branches to try — which one do you try first?


Usually… whichever comes first. Arbitrary order.


What if we could rank our choices and always try the most promising one?
That’s the core idea behind A*.

title: A* Search
text:
Motivating Example: Navigation
You’re in a city. You want to go from A to B.


Option 1 — Blind search:
Expand every reachable node equally.
Eventually you’ll find B… maybe.



A broad, wasteful search frontier spreading in all directions



Option 2 — Guided search:
Prefer nodes that are closer to B and cheaply reached.



A more focussed elliptical search frontier growing towards the destination





Recap: In backtracking, when you have multiple branches to try — which one do you try first?


Its arbitrary. A* gives us a principled way to rank our choices and always pick the best one first.

title: A* Search
text:
Two Algorithms to Know First
Before A*, let’s name two simpler cousins:



Algorithm
Strategy
Blind to…




BFS
Expand shallowest node first
Cost of edges


Dijkstra’s
Expand cheapest-cost node first
Direction to goal


A*
Expand best estimated total cost
Nothing — uses both!





A* = Dijkstra’s + a compass pointing toward the goal.

title: A* Search
text:
The Key Insight: Two Costs
For every node \(n\) we’re considering, A* tracks:
\[f(n) = g(n) + h(n)\]


\(g(n)\)
Cost so far
How much did it cost to reach this node from the start?
(exact — we know this)

\(h(n)\)
Estimated cost ahead
How far are we still from the goal?
(a guess — a heuristic)

\(f(n)\)
Total estimated cost
Our best estimate of the whole path cost through \(n\).
(what A* uses to decide)



Question: \(g\) is exact. \(h\) is a guess. Why not just use \(g\) and be precise?

title: A* Search
section: The Heuristic \(h(n)\): A Guess With Rules
text:
The Heuristic \(h(n)\): A Guess With Rules
\(h(n)\) is an estimate of the cost from \(n\) to the goal.
You get to design it — but it must follow one key rule.
Admissibility rule: \(h(n)\) must never overestimate the true cost.
\[h(n) \leq h^*(n) \quad \text{(true cost to goal)}\]

Question: Why would overestimating be a problem?
Think: if \(h\) overestimates, what might A* skip?


It might skip the optimal path — mistakenly thinking it’s too expensive.

title: A* Search
text:
Classic Heuristic: Straight-Line Distance
For navigation on a map, a natural heuristic is:
\[h(n) = \text{straight-line distance from } n \text{ to goal}\]
Question: Is straight-line distance admissible? Can the real road ever be shorter than a straight line?

No! Roads can only be at least as long as the straight line.
So straight-line distance never overestimates. ✅ Admissible.


Admissibility is easy to reason about intuitively:
“Could the real cost ever be less than my guess?”
If the answer is no, you’re admissible.

title: A* Search
text:
How A* Works: The Algorithm
def search(graph):
  open_set = priority_queue()  # ordered by f(n)
  start = graph.start_node
  f[start] = g[start] + h[start]
  open_set.add(start, f[start])  # add the start node with priority value f

  while open_set is not empty:
    node = open_set.pop()  # get the node with lowest f(n)
    if node == goal:
      return reconstruct_path(node) # found goal! reconstruct path back to source
    for neighbor in graph.neighbors(node):
      if neighbor not in open_set:
        g[neighbor] = g[node] + cost(node, neighbor)
        f[neighbor] = g[neighbor] + h[neighbor]
        open_set.add(neighbor, f[neighbor])
  return FAILURE

Notice: we only update a node if we found a better path to it.

section: Why A* Doesn’t Miss the Optimal Path
text:
Why A* Doesn’t Miss the Optimal Path

Key guarantee: If \(h\) is admissible, A* will find the optimal path.

Intuition:

The optimal path has some true cost \(C^*\)
Any unexplored node on the optimal path has \(f \leq C^*\)
(because \(h\) never overestimates what remains)
A* only stops when it pops the goal from the queue
When the goal is popped, its \(g\) value is the optimal cost



Question: What would happen if we used \(h = 0\) for everything?
(i.e., we pretend there’s no remaining cost)



\(h = 0\) → \(f = g\) → A* becomes Dijkstra’s! Still correct, just slower.

title: A* Search
text:
Heuristic Quality Matters
All admissible heuristics give correct answers.
But better heuristics give faster answers.

Question: Which heuristic explores fewer nodes — a good one or a weak one?


A stronger \(h\) (closer to the true cost) → fewer nodes expanded → faster.



Heuristic
Behavior




\(h = 0\)

\(h = h^*\) (perfect)
Only explores nodes on the optimal path


\(h > h^*\) (inadmissible)
Fast, but may miss optimal






The sweet spot: as close to \(h^*\) as possible without going over.

title: A* Search
text:
Designing Heuristics: Relaxed Problems
A powerful technique: solve an easier version of the problem.

“What if some constraints didn’t exist?”


8-Puzzle example: move tiles to reach goal configuration.


START               GOAL

+---+---+---+       +---+---+---+
| 7 | 2 | 4 |       | 1 | 2 | 3 |
+---+---+---+       +---+---+---+
| 5 |   | 6 |       | 4 | 5 | 6 |
+---+---+---+       +---+---+---+
| 8 | 3 | 1 |       | 7 | 8 |   |
+---+---+---+       +---+---+---+

Possible heuristics:

\(h_1\): Misplaced tiles — count tiles not in their goal position
(Relaxation: tiles can teleport anywhere)
\(h_2\): Manhattan distance — sum of how far each tile needs to move
(Relaxation: tiles can pass through each other)






Question: Which is stronger, \(h_1\) or \(h_2\)?
Can you give an example where they differ?

title: A* Search
text:
Dominance: Comparing Heuristics
We say \(h_2\) dominates \(h_1\) if:
\[h_2(n) \geq h_1(n) \quad \text{for all } n\]
(and both are admissible)

A dominating heuristic always expands no more nodes than the dominated one.
Manhattan distance dominates misplaced tiles for the 8-puzzle.



Question: If you have two admissible heuristics \(h_1\) and \(h_2\), can you combine them?
How?



Yes! \(h(n) = \max(h_1(n), h_2(n))\) is admissible and dominates both.

title: A* Search
text:
Consistency (a Stronger Property)
Admissibility: \(h(n) \leq\) true cost from \(n\) to goal.
Consistency (also called monotonicity): for every edge \(n \to m\):
\[h(n) \leq \text{cost}(n \to m) + h(m)\]

Question: What does this inequality look like geometrically?
(Hint: think triangle)


It’s the triangle inequality — the heuristic can’t drop faster than the actual edge cost.

Consistency → Admissibility (but not vice versa).
With a consistent heuristic, every node is expanded at most once — no re-expansion!

title: A* Search
text:
A* vs. Dijkstra’s: Visualized


Dijkstra’s (\(h = 0\))
Expands in uniform rings of equal cost — like ripples in a pond.
Explores in all directions equally.


A* (good \(h\))
Expands in an ellipse stretching toward the goal.
Focuses exploration where it matters.




Question: When would A* and Dijkstra’s expand the same set of nodes?



When the goal is the closest node — or when \(h\) gives no useful information about direction.

title: Introduction to Dynamic Programming
text:
What Is Dynamic Programming?
Dynamic Programming (DP) is a technique for solving problems by:

Breaking them into overlapping subproblems
Solving each subproblem once
Storing the result so it’s never recomputed




DP is NOT:

A data structure
A specific algorithm
Only for hard problems




DP IS:

A way of thinking about recursion
An optimisation of repeated work
Recursion + memory





One-liner: “Remember what you’ve already solved.”

title: Introduction to Dynamic Programming
text:
The Two Ingredients of DP
Every DP problem requires exactly two things:



1. Optimal Substructure
The optimal solution to the problem contains optimal solutions to its subproblems.

“I can build the best answer from the best answers to smaller versions.”




2. Overlapping Subproblems
The same subproblems appear again and again during recursion.

“I keep solving the same smaller problems repeatedly — let me cache them.”




If both conditions hold → DP will help you.

Merge Sort splits [1..n] into [1..n/2] and [n/2+1..n]. Those halves never overlap.
Fibonacci needs fib(4) to compute both fib(5) and fib(6). They do overlap.

title: Introduction to Dynamic Programming
Introduction to Dynamic Programming
text:
Why Is It So Slow?
The call tree for fib(6) has 25 nodes, even though there are only 7 distinct subproblems (fib(0)…fib(6)).

fib(6) call treefib(3) alone is called 3 times, fib(2) is called 5 times.

This is the overlapping subproblems problem.
The fix? Store results the first time. Memoisation.

title: Introduction to Dynamic Programming
text:
Fibonacci — Top-Down DP (Memoisation)
Add a cache. If we’ve seen it before, return the stored answer.
memo = {}
def fib_memo(n):
    if n in memo:
        return memo[n]          # ← cache hit!
    if n <= 1:
        return n

    memo[n] = fib_memo(n-1) + fib_memo(n-2)  # ← store result in cache
    return memo[n]
Now fib(5) only ever computes each value once:
fib(5) → fib(4) → fib(3) → fib(2) → fib(1) = 1
                                   → fib(0) = 0
                         → fib(1) = 1  [cached: skip]
               → fib(2) = 1  [cached: skip]
         → fib(3) = 2  [cached: skip]
Time: O(n) — Space: O(n)

Instead of recursing top-down, fill a table from the base cases upward.

    if n <= 1:

    dp = [0] * (n + 1)
    dp[0] = 0
    dp[1] = 1

    for i in range(2, n + 1):
        dp[i] = dp[i-1] + dp[i-2]   # ← use already-computed values

    return dp[n]

title: Introduction to Dynamic Programming
text:
Problem: Climbing Stairs

You’re climbing a staircase with n steps.
Each move you can climb 1 or 2 steps.
How many distinct ways can you reach the top?


Examples:

n = 1: [1] → 1 way
n = 2: [1+1], [2] → 2 ways
n = 3: [1+1+1], [1+2], [2+1] → 3 ways
n = 4: [1+1+1+1], [1+1+2], [1+2+1], [2+1+1], [2+2] → 5 ways

Notice anything?


1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 13, ... — it’s Fibonacci!

title: Introduction to Dynamic Programming
text:
Climbing Stairs — Recurrence
Key insight: to reach step n, you came from either:

step n-1 (took a 1-step), or
step n-2 (took a 2-step)

So: ways(n) = ways(n-1) + ways(n-2)

def climb_stairs(n):
    if n <= 2:
        return n

    dp = [0] * (n + 1)
    dp[1] = 1   # one way to reach step 1
    dp[2] = 2   # two ways to reach step 2

    for i in range(3, n + 1):
        dp[i] = dp[i-1] + dp[i-2]

    return dp[n]


This problem teaches the core DP pattern: define dp[i] = answer for subproblem of size i, build up from base cases.

title: Introduction to Dynamic Programming
text:
Problem: Coin Change

You have coins of denominations [1, 5, 6, 9].
What is the minimum number of coins to make amount n = 11?

Greedy fails here! Greedy picks 9 first → 9 + 1 + 1 = 3 coins.
But optimal is 5 + 6 = 2 coins. ✓
Why DP? To make amount n, we can use any coin c, and then we need to make n - c with minimum coins. The subproblems overlap heavily.

title: Introduction to Dynamic Programming
text:
Coin Change — Recurrence
Let dp[i] = minimum coins needed to make amount i.
Recurrence: \[dp[i] = 1 + \min_{c \in \text{coins}} dp[i - c] \quad \text{for } i \geq c\]
Base case: dp[0] = 0 (zero coins needed to make 0)
Intuition: for each amount, try every coin and take the best option.

Coin Change — Code
def coin_change(coins, amount):
    INF = float('inf')
    dp = [INF] * (amount + 1)
    dp[0] = 0   # base case

    for i in range(1, amount + 1):
        for coin in coins:
            if coin <= i and dp[i - coin] != INF:
                dp[i] = min(dp[i], dp[i - coin] + 1)

    return dp[amount] if dp[amount] != INF else -1

print(coin_change([1, 5, 6, 9], 11))  # → 2
print(coin_change([2], 3))            # → -1 (impossible)
Time: O(amount × |coins|)
Space: O(amount)

title: Introduction to Dynamic Programming
text:
Problem: Longest Common Subsequence (LCS)

Given two strings, find the length of their longest common subsequence.

A subsequence keeps characters in order but skips some.
Example:
s1 = "ABCBDAB"
s2 = "BDCABA"

LCS = "BCBA"  (length 4)
B_C_B_A appears in both strings (in order, not necessarily contiguous).
Applications: diff tools (git diff!), DNA sequence alignment, spell checking.

title: Introduction to Dynamic Programming
text:
LCS — Recurrence
Define dp[i][j] = LCS length of s1[0..i-1] and s2[0..j-1].
Recurrence:
\(dp[i][j] = \begin{cases} dp[i-1][j-1] + 1 & \text{if } s1[i-1] = s2[j-1] \\ \max(dp[i-1][j],\ dp[i][j-1]) & \text{otherwise} \end{cases}\)
Intuition:

Characters match → extend the LCS by 1
Characters don’t match → take the better of skipping from either string

Base cases: dp[0][j] = 0, dp[i][0] = 0 (empty string has no common subsequence)

\(dp[i][j] = \begin{cases} dp[i-1][j-1] + 1 & \text{if } s1[i-1] = s2[j-1] \\ \max(dp[i-1][j],\ dp[i][j-1]) & \text{otherwise} \end{cases}\)

Knapsack — Code
def knapsack(weights, values, W):
    n = len(weights)
    dp = [[0] * (W + 1) for _ in range(n + 1)]

    for i in range(1, n + 1):
        wt, val = weights[i-1], values[i-1]
        for w in range(W + 1):
            # Option 1: skip item i
            dp[i][w] = dp[i-1][w]

            # Option 2: take item i (if it fits)
            if wt <= w:
                dp[i][w] = max(dp[i][w], dp[i-1][w - wt] + val)

    return dp[n][W]

The DP Design Process
When you see a new problem, ask these questions in order:

Can I define the problem recursively?
→ “What smaller versions of this problem do I need?”
Do subproblems overlap?
→ Draw the recursion tree. Are the same calls repeated?
What is my dp[...] state?
→ What information fully describes a subproblem?
What is the recurrence?
→ How does dp[i] (or dp[i][j]) depend on smaller states?
What are the base cases?
→ What are the smallest subproblems I can answer directly?
In what order should I fill the table?
→ Each cell must be computed after the cells it depends on.

title: Randomized Algorithms
text:
The Core Idea
We’ve been designing algorithms that are deterministic — same input, same exact steps, same output every time.

What if we let the algorithm flip coins?


Surprisingly, this can be:

Simpler to implement
Faster in practice
Harder to fool by adversaries
The only known approach for some problems

title: Randomized Algorithms
text:
Two Flavors of Randomized Algorithms


Las Vegas 🎰
Always gives the correct answer.
Running time varies randomly.
“We’ll get there — just not sure when.”
Example: Randomized QuickSort

Monte Carlo 🎲
Always runs in bounded time.
Answer may be wrong with small probability.
“We’re probably right.”
Example: Bloom filters, primality testing



Most randomized algorithms we’ll see today are Monte Carlo — tunable error probability.

title: Randomized Algorithms
text:
Intuition: Why Randomness Helps
Imagine an adversary who knows your algorithm and picks the worst-case input.


Deterministic QuickSort: Always pick first element as pivot → adversary gives sorted array → O(n²) every time




Randomized QuickSort: Pick pivot randomly → adversary can’t predict your choice → O(n log n) expected no matter what



Key insight: Randomness breaks the adversary’s ability to plan against you.

title: Randomized Algorithms
text:
Randomized Pivot Selection
import random

def quicksort(A, lo, hi):
    if lo < hi:
        pivot_idx = random.randint(lo, hi)   # random pivot!
        A[lo], A[pivot_idx] = A[pivot_idx], A[lo]
        p = partition(A, lo, hi)
        quicksort(A, lo, p - 1)
        quicksort(A, p + 1, hi)

One-line change. Huge difference.

Expected time: O(n log n) on any input
Worst case still O(n²) — but now astronomically unlikely
No adversary can engineer a bad case without knowing your coin flips

title: Randomized Algorithms
section: Intuition for Expected O(n log n)
text:
Intuition for Expected O(n log n)
Think about any two elements \(x\) and \(y\) in the array.

When do they get compared? Only when one of them is chosen as a pivot before either is “separated” from the other by an earlier partition.


The probability that \(x\) and \(y\) are ever compared = \(\frac{2}{\text{elements between them (inclusive)}}\)


Summing over all pairs → O(n log n) expected comparisons total.
(This is the key insight — we don’t need to trace through recursion!)

title: Randomized Algorithms
text:
The Fingerprinting Idea
Problem: You have a 10 GB file. Your friend has a 10 GB file. Are they the same?

Naive: Send the whole file.


Smart: Compute a short fingerprint (hash) of each file. Compare fingerprints.


A good hash function maps a big object → small digest such that:

Same object → same hash (always)
Different objects → same hash (almost never)



This is the foundation of Rabin-Karp and Bloom Filters.

title: Randomized Algorithms
text:
The Pattern Matching Problem
Input: Text \(T\) of length \(n\), Pattern \(P\) of length \(m\)
Output: All positions in \(T\) where \(P\) occurs
T = "the cat sat on the mat"
P = "at"

Matches at positions: 5, 9, 20

Naive approach: Slide \(P\) over \(T\), compare character by character.
Worst case: O(nm) — think T = “aaaa…a”, P = “aaa…ab”

title: Randomized Algorithms
text:
Rabin-Karp: The Key Idea
Instead of comparing strings character-by-character, compare their hashes.


Compute hash of pattern \(P\) → \(h_P\)
Slide a window of length \(m\) over \(T\)
At each position, compute hash of window → \(h_W\)
If \(h_W = h_P\) → probably a match (verify to be sure)
If \(h_W \neq h_P\) → definitely not a match



Magic: We can update the window hash in O(1) using a rolling hash.

title: Randomized Algorithms
text:
Rolling Hash: The Mechanism
Treat each window as a number in base \(b\) (e.g., \(b = 256\) for ASCII):
\[h(\text{"cat"}) = \text{'c'} \cdot b^2 + \text{'a'} \cdot b^1 + \text{'t'} \cdot b^0 \pmod{q}\]

When the window slides right by one character:
\[h_{\text{new}} = \left( h_{\text{old}} - T[i] \cdot b^{m-1} \right) \cdot b + T[i+m] \pmod{q}\]


\(q\) is a large prime to prevent overflow and reduce collisions.






Tip


Intuition: Subtract the leftmost character’s contribution, shift everything left, add the new rightmost character. O(1) per step!

title: Randomized Algorithms
Randomized Algorithms
text:
The Membership Problem
Question: Is element \(x\) in set \(S\)?

Exact solutions:

Hash table: O(1) average, but stores all elements
For millions of URLs, this needs gigabytes of RAM



What if we allow a small error?

“Is this URL in our blocklist?”
Acceptable: occasionally say “yes” when it’s actually “no”
Not acceptable: say “no” when it’s actually “yes”

title: Randomized Algorithms
text:
Bloom Filter: The Structure
A Bloom filter is a bit array of \(m\) bits (all initially 0) + \(k\) hash functions.

Insert element \(x\):
Hash \(x\) with each of \(k\) functions → set those \(k\) bits to 1


Query element \(x\):
Hash \(x\) → check those \(k\) bits

All 1? → probably in set
Any 0? → definitely not in set

           0 1 1 0 0 1 0 1 0 0

Query “cat”: bits 2,7 → both 1 ✅ probably yes
Query “rat”: \(h_1\)=1, \(h_2\)=4 → bit 4 is 0 ❌ definitely no
Query “eel”: \(h_1\)=1, \(h_2\)=5 → both 1… false positive!









Warning


False positives happen when an element “accidentally” maps to all set bits.
False negatives are impossible — if you inserted it, those bits stay 1.

title: Randomized Algorithms
text:
Tuning the Error Rate
The false positive rate depends on:

\(m\) — number of bits (bigger → fewer collisions)
\(n\) — number of elements inserted
\(k\) — number of hash functions


\[\text{False positive rate} \approx \left(1 - e^{-kn/m}\right)^k\]


Optimal \(k\) (minimizes false positives): \(k = \frac{m}{n} \ln 2 \approx 0.7 \cdot \frac{m}{n}\)








Tip


Rule of thumb: ~10 bits per element → ~1% false positive rate with optimal \(k \approx 7\) hash functions.

title: Randomized Algorithms
text:
Real-World Bloom Filter Uses

Browsers (Chrome): Safe Browsing — is this URL malicious? (Bloom filter downloaded locally, rare positives trigger a real server lookup)
Databases (Cassandra, HBase): “Does this key exist anywhere before we do a disk seek?”
Spell checkers: Is this word in the dictionary?
Network routers: Duplicate packet detection
CDNs: Track which objects to cache


Common theme: A tiny, fast “probably yes/definitely no” check that saves expensive lookups.

title: Randomized Algorithms
text:
Limitations of Bloom Filters


Can’t do:

Delete elements (without extensions)
Return the element itself
Count occurrences
Enumerate members


Variants that extend this:

Counting Bloom Filter: supports deletes
Cuckoo Filter: also supports deletes, better cache performance
HyperLogLog: count distinct elements approximately

title: Randomized Algorithms
text:
Motivation: Ordered Dictionaries
A hash table gives O(1) lookup but no ordering.
Sorted arrays give O(log n) search but O(n) insert.
Balanced BSTs give O(log n) for both but are complex to implement correctly (rotations!).

Skip List: A randomized data structure achieving O(log n) expected for search, insert, delete — with a beautifully simple idea.

title: Randomized Algorithms
text:
The Skip List Idea
Start with a sorted linked list. Search is O(n) — we have to walk it.

What if we add “express lanes”?


Level 1: 1 ──> 3 ──> 4 ──> 6 ──> 7 ──> 8 ──> 9
Level 2: 1 ────────> 4 ────────> 7 ────────> 9
Level 3: 1 ────────────────────────────────> 9


Search for 6:

Start at level 3: 1 → 9 (too far), drop down
Level 2: 1 → 4 → 7 (overshot), drop down
Level 1: 4 → 6 ✓



3 steps instead of 6

title: Randomized Algorithms
text:
How Levels Are Assigned
When inserting a new element, flip a coin repeatedly:
def random_level(max_level, p=0.5):
    level = 1
    while random.random() < p and level < max_level:
        level += 1
    return level


Each element appears on level 1 (always)
Promoted to level 2 with probability \(p\)
Promoted to level 3 with probability \(p^2\)
…



Expected number of levels: \(\log_{1/p} n\)
With \(p = 0.5\): ~\(\log_2 n\) levels — like a balanced BST, but no balancing code!
